seo.shortDescription: Searchable 2026 U.S. tariff table for every HTS Chapter 91 line: wrist watches, clocks, movements, cases, straps and parts. Watch base rates are compound (per movement + % on the case, strap and battery); since July 24, 2026 Swiss and Japanese watches pay 12.5% of value in total, EU watches 10%, Chinese watches the base rate + 20%.
keywords: clocks and watches and parts thereof tariff
clocks and watches and parts thereof import duty rates

overview.intro:
Chapter 91 covers **wrist and pocket watches** (9101 with a case of precious metal, 9102 all others), **clocks** (9103–9105), time recorders and parking meters (9106), time switches (9107), **watch and clock movements** (9108–9110), cases (9111–9112), **watch straps and bracelets** (9113) and other parts (9114). Of its 177 rate lines, 21 are Free and 125 carry a **compound rate**: a charge per movement plus percentages on the **case**, the **strap, band or bracelet** and the **battery**, each on its own value. A steel automatic watch with over 17 jewels and a steel bracelet (9102.21.70) pays $1.53 + 4.2% of the case value + 9.8% of the bracelet value. Many mechanical watches with gold or platinum cases (9101.21.50, 9101.29.90, 9101.91 and most of 9101.99) are Free.

The U.S. imported **$6.77B** of Chapter 91 goods in 2025, 12.6% less than in 2024. **Switzerland** supplied $5.52B (81.6%), almost all of it watches, ahead of Japan ($445M) and China ($400M). Watches (9101 and 9102) were 91% of the total.

Since **July 24, 2026** the Section 301 tariff on 60 economies applies by country. **Swiss and Japanese** goods pay **12.5% in total** where their base rate is lower, and **EU and Taiwanese** goods pay **10% in total**. For a compound watch rate this means a flat 12.5% or 10% of the watch's value (note 52(k)). Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore and Hong Kong pay the base rate **+12.5%**; the UK, India, Malaysia and non-USMCA goods of Mexico and Canada pay **+10%**. **China** pays the base rate + 12.5% plus the 7.5% List 4A duty on most watches and parts, or the 25% List 3 duty on instrument-panel clocks, time recorders and time switches. USMCA-qualifying goods pay nothing. The IEEPA duties (39% on Swiss goods from August 7, 2025, then 15% in total) ended **February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ended July 23, 2026. No Section 232 duty and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 91 product.

productGroups.label: Wrist watches, pocket watches and other watches, including stop watches, with case of precious metal or of metal clad with precious metal
productGroups.blurb: Watches with a case wholly of gold, silver, platinum or metal clad with precious metal (chapter note 2). Electric watches with hands pay a compound rate (41¢–87¢ + 4.4%–6.25% on case and strap + 3.7%–5.3% on the battery); mechanical watches with over 17 jewels and most pocket watches are Free, their straps 3.1%.
productGroups.rateSummary: Free · 3.1% · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Wrist watches, pocket watches and other watches, including stop watches, other than those of heading 9101
productGroups.blurb: Watches with a case of steel, titanium, ceramic, plastic or any other material that is not precious metal. Almost every line is compound: a charge per movement, plus percentages on the case, the strap, band or bracelet and the battery. 9102.21 (automatic) and 9102.11 (quartz with hands) are the largest lines.
productGroups.rateSummary: Free · 14% · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Clocks with watch movements, excluding clocks of heading 9104
productGroups.blurb: Clocks built around a watch movement, such as small travel and desk clocks, other than vehicle clocks. Compound rates on the movement, case and battery.
productGroups.rateSummary: compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Instrument panel clocks and clocks of a similar type for vehicles, aircraft, spacecraft or vessels
productGroups.blurb: Instrument-panel clocks for cars, aircraft, spacecraft and vessels. Compound rates; on China List 3 (25%) except 9104.00.60. Civil-aircraft clocks meeting general note 6 are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.
productGroups.rateSummary: 30¢ each + 6.4% · 30¢ each + 4.3% · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Other clocks
productGroups.blurb: Alarm clocks, wall clocks and other clocks, including marine chronometers. Mostly per-clock + % on the case (and battery).
productGroups.rateSummary: 15¢ each + 6.4% · 23¢ each + 3.2% · 30¢ each + 4.3% · 17¢ each + 2.5% + 1¢/jewel · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Time of day recording apparatus and apparatus for measuring, recording or otherwise indicating intervals of time, with clock or watch movement or with synchronous motor (for example, time registers, time-recorders)
productGroups.blurb: Time clocks for employees, parking meters, time locks and interval timers with a clock or watch movement or a synchronous motor. China List 3 (25%).
productGroups.rateSummary: 36¢ each + 5.6% + 2¢/jewel · 15¢ each + 2.3% + 0.8¢/jewel · 3.9% · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Time switches with clock or watch movement or with synchronous motor
productGroups.blurb: Time switches with a clock movement or synchronous motor, such as appliance and lighting timers. Mostly from Mexico, Free under USMCA; China List 3 (25%).

productGroups.label: Watch movements, complete and assembled
productGroups.blurb: Complete, assembled watch movements (12 mm thick and 50 mm wide at most). Per-movement rates of 25¢–$2.16, plus % on the battery for quartz; automatic movements are Free.
productGroups.rateSummary: Free · 29¢ each · 25¢ each · 57¢ each · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Clock movements, complete and assembled
productGroups.blurb: Complete, assembled clock movements. Per-movement rates, plus % on the movement or battery for the larger ones.
productGroups.rateSummary: 20¢ each · 15¢ each + 6.4% · 30¢ each + 4.3% · compound: per piece + % on movement, case, strap or battery

productGroups.label: Complete watch or clock movements, unassembled or partly assembled (movement sets); incomplete watch or clock movements, assembled; rough watch or clock movements
productGroups.blurb: Movement sets (unassembled), incomplete and rough movements, and movement parts fastened together. A movement set pays the rate of the complete movement; incomplete or rough watch movements 9%.
productGroups.rateSummary: 9% · 4.2% · movement sets at the complete movement's rate

productGroups.label: Watch cases and parts thereof
productGroups.blurb: Watch cases and their parts (bezels, backs, centers). Gold or silver cases 12¢ + 4.8%; base-metal cases up to 3.6¢ + 7.6%.

productGroups.label: Clock cases and cases of a similar type for other goods of this chapter, and parts thereof
productGroups.blurb: Clock cases and their parts. 3.5% (metal) to 5.5%.

productGroups.label: Watch straps, watch bands and watch bracelets, and parts thereof
productGroups.blurb: Watch straps, bands and bracelets imported on their own (with the watch they go to 9101/9102). Precious metal 4.5%, base metal 11.2% (parts 8.8%), textile 7.2%, leather, rubber and other 1.8%.

productGroups.label: Other clock or watch parts
productGroups.blurb: Other clock and watch parts: dials, plates and bridges, jewels (Free), springs and hairsprings, assemblies, hands and crowns.

rateTable.note: Rates shown in grey are inherited from the parent heading. HTSUS states a duty once on the 8-digit line and leaves the 10-digit statistical lines blank; this table resolves each line to the rate that actually applies to it.

workedExamples.title: Swiss steel automatic watch on a rubber strap
workedExamples.body: A $5,000 automatic watch with a stainless-steel case and over 17 jewels; the case is worth $1,500 and the strap $100. The base rate is $1.53 for the movement + 4.2% of the case ($63) + 2% of the strap ($2) = **$66.53**. The entry reports the movement, case and strap on their own statistical suffixes (9102.21.9010, .9020, .9030) with their values, as CBP ruled for this line in NY N362026; the tariff calculator takes the same component values. That is 1.3% of the value, below 12.5%, so for a Swiss watch heading 9903.05.74 replaces it: **12.5% × $5,000 = $625**. The same watch pays $625 from Japan, $500 from Germany (10% in total), $566.53 from the UK (base + 10%) and $1,066.53 from China (base + 12.5% + 7.5%). Before 2025 it paid $66.53. From August 7 to November 13, 2025 it paid $2,016.53 (base + 39%), then $750 (15% in total) until February 23, 2026, then $566.53 (base + 10% Section 122) until July 23, 2026.

workedExamples.title: Swiss gold automatic watch
workedExamples.body: A $30,000 automatic watch with an 18-karat gold case and over 17 jewels: the watch line is **Free**, and its strap, reported separately (9101.21.10 or 9101.21.30), pays 3.1%. Both are below 12.5%, so a Swiss watch pays **12.5% of $30,000 = $3,750** (9903.05.74). From Japan it is also $3,750, from the EU $3,000 and from China $6,000 (12.5% + 7.5%).

workedExamples.title: Japanese quartz analog watch
workedExamples.body: A $200 battery watch with hands, a steel case worth $60, a leather strap worth $20 and a $1 battery. The base rate is 40¢ + 8.5% of the case ($5.10) + 2.8% of the strap ($0.56) + 5.3% of the battery ($0.05) = **$6.11** (3.1%). Japan pays **12.5% in total = $25** (9903.05.49). The same watch pays $46.11 from China ($6.11 + $25 + $15 List 4A), $31.11 from Thailand, Vietnam or Hong Kong, $26.11 from the UK or non-USMCA Mexico, $20 from the EU and nothing if it qualifies for USMCA.

workedExamples.title: Watch movement sets and movement parts from China
workedExamples.body: Unassembled movement sets pay **"the rate applicable to the complete, assembled movement"**, so the importer names the movement line. For 100 sets of a 17-plus-jewel movement (9108.90.90, $1.50 each), worth $5,000, the base is $150; China adds 12.5% ($625) and 7.5% List 4A ($375): **$1,150**. Movement parts fastened together (9110.90.40) pay 4.3% + 1.7¢ per jewel + 0.2¢ per other piece: $2,000 of parts with 1,700 jewels and 5,000 other pieces owe $124.90. If the parts include a plate, the duty is capped at the duty on the complete movement, for example $29 for 100 movements of 9108.90.10 (29¢ each).

workedExamples.title: Mexican time switches under USMCA
workedExamples.body: Time switches (9107) were Mexico's main Chapter 91 export to the U.S. ($69.8M in 2025). They pay 15¢ each + 4% + 2.5¢ per jewel, and +10% under Section 301 (9903.05.55), unless they qualify for USMCA. A qualifying switch enters **Free** with no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). The same switch from China pays the base rate + 12.5% + 25% (List 3).

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) clock or watch glasses or weights (classified by material); (b) watch chains (heading 7113 or 7117); (c) parts of general use of base metal (section XV), similar goods of plastics (chapter 39) or of precious metal (generally heading 7115) — clock or watch springs are, however, classified in heading 9114; (d) bearing balls (7326 or 8482); (e) articles of heading 8412 constructed to work without an escapement; (f) ball bearings (8482); or (g) articles of chapter 85 not yet assembled into watch or clock movements or into parts suitable solely or principally for them.

**Note 2.** Heading 9101 covers only watches with case wholly of precious metal or of metal clad with precious metal, or of those materials combined with natural or cultured pearls or precious or semiprecious stones of headings 7101 to 7104. Watches with case of base metal inlaid with precious metal fall in heading 9102.

**Note 3.** "Watch movements" means devices regulated by a balance wheel and hairspring, quartz crystal or any other system capable of determining intervals of time, with a display or a system to which a mechanical display can be incorporated, not exceeding 12 mm in thickness and 50 mm in width, length or diameter.

**Note 4.** Except as provided in note 1, movements and other parts suitable for use both in clocks or watches and in other articles (for example, precision instruments) are classified in this chapter.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** Definitions: "watches" are timepieces of a kind for wearing or carrying on the person (a timepiece with a stand is not a watch); "cases" include inner and outer cases and their parts; "jewels" include substitutes for jewels; "clock movements" exceed 12 mm in thickness or 50 mm in width; and the note defines movement sets, incomplete movements and rough movements.

**2.** Straps, bands and bracelets entered with wrist watches and of a kind normally sold with them are classified with the watch in 9101 or 9102; otherwise in heading 9113.

**3.** Batteries entered with battery-powered watches, clocks or movements, and intended for use with them, are classified with the watch, clock or movement; otherwise in heading 8506 or 8507.

**4. Special marking requirements.** Any movement or case, imported separately or in a watch or clock, may not be entered unless conspicuously and indelibly marked by cutting, die-sinking, engraving, stamping or mold-marking: watch movements on a bridge or top plate with the country of manufacture, the name of the manufacturer or purchaser and, in words, the number of jewels; clock movements with the country, the manufacturer or purchaser and the number of jewels; watch cases inside or outside the back with the country and the manufacturer or purchaser; clock cases on the back with the country. Movements with opto-electronic display only, and their cases, are excepted.

**5. Products of insular possessions.** Watches and watch movements assembled in the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam or American Samoa may enter free of duty regardless of foreign content, within annual quantities and licenses set jointly by the Secretaries of Commerce and the Interior (15 CFR part 303), unless they contain material of a column 2 country.

**Statistical note 1.** Duties on many watches, clocks and movements are calculated by constructively separating the article into its components, each separately valued and reported under its own statistical suffix (for example movement 10, case 20, strap, band or bracelet 30, battery 40); the component values must add up to the value of the article, and a component that is not in the shipment is reported with zero quantity and value.

seo.title: Swiss Watch Tariff 2026 & HTS Chapter 91 Tariff Updates: Section 301, IEEPA End, Japan & China Rates | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. watch and clock imports since January 2025: the Swiss 39% reciprocal tariff and the 15% deal rate (ended February 24, 2026), the 10% Section 122 surcharge (ended July 23), and since July 24, 2026 the Section 301 rates — Swiss and Japanese watches 12.5% in total, EU 10%, China base + 20% — with Federal Register citations.
keywords: clocks and watches and parts thereof tariff
switzerland tariff on clocks and watches and parts thereof

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 91 base rate changed**, so the compound watch rates (a charge per movement plus percentages on the case, strap and battery) are the same as before 2025.

Everything that changed sits on top. In 2025 the IEEPA reciprocal tariff hit watches with no exemption: **Swiss watches paid 39% on top of the base rate from August 7, 2025**, cut to **15% in total from November 14, 2025** under the U.S.–Switzerland framework. Japanese and EU watches paid 15% in total, and Chinese watches up to 125% + 20% for five weeks in spring 2025. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**. The 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** a **Section 301 tariff** applies by country: Swiss and Japanese watches pay **12.5% of value in total**, EU and Taiwanese ones 10%; Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore and Hong Kong add 12.5% to the base rate, the UK, India, Malaysia and non-USMCA goods of Mexico and Canada 10%. China still adds the List 4A (7.5%) or List 3 (25%) duty on top of its 12.5%.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 91 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemption lists, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 List 3 and List 4A duties, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. The de minimis suspension, the IEEPA refund process and the scheduled Nicaragua tariff are listed for reference. No Section 232 duty, no Canada Section 338 list and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 91 product. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: Swiss goods pay 12.5% in total where the base rate is below 12.5% (9903.05.74), and only the base rate where it is 12.5% or more (9903.05.73). Under note 52(k) the ad valorem equivalent of a compound watch rate is the base-rate duty divided by the customs value. For nearly every watch it is well below that figure (a $5,000 steel automatic watch owes $66.53 at the base rate, 1.3%), so the watch pays the flat percentage of its whole value. Only one exemption list names Chapter 91 lines: civil-aircraft goods that meet general note 6 (note 52(d), 9903.05.88), which covers instrument-panel clocks of 9104.00.05–9104.00.60 and clock movements of 9109.10.50, 9109.10.60 and 9109.90.20. No Chapter 91 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). Switzerland's exception list (note 52(j)(3), 9903.05.98) names no watch, clock or part. The 39% IEEPA rate of August 7, 2025 (15% in total from November 14, 2025) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A Swiss watch pays 12.5% of its value whatever its jewels, case or strap: $625 on a $5,000 steel automatic, $3,750 on a $30,000 gold one. Swiss watch movements, straps and parts pay 12.5% too.

inEffect.exemption: Japanese goods pay 12.5% in total where the base rate is below 12.5% (9903.05.49). Under note 52(k) the ad valorem equivalent of a compound watch rate is the base-rate duty divided by the customs value. For nearly every watch it is well below that figure (a $5,000 steel automatic watch owes $66.53 at the base rate, 1.3%), so the watch pays the flat percentage of its whole value. Only one exemption list names Chapter 91 lines: civil-aircraft goods that meet general note 6 (note 52(d), 9903.05.88), which covers instrument-panel clocks of 9104.00.05–9104.00.60 and clock movements of 9109.10.50, 9109.10.60 and 9109.90.20. No Chapter 91 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). The 15%-in-total IEEPA rate ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A $200 Japanese quartz watch pays $25 (12.5%); a $1,000 automatic $125. Japanese watch movements pay 12.5% of their value.

inEffect.exemption: Two Section 301 actions stack. The 2026 action adds +12.5% (9903.05.31). The 2018–2019 China lists add +7.5% (List 4A, 9903.88.15) on most watches, watch and clock movements, cases, straps and parts, or +25% (List 3, 9903.88.03) on instrument-panel clocks (9104.00.05–9104.00.50), time recorders, parking meters and interval timers (9106) and time switches (9107). Some lines are on neither list: battery and opto-electronic alarm, wall and other clocks (9105.11, 9105.21, 9105.91, 9105.19.40, 9105.29.40, 9105.99.50), clocks with watch movements of 9103.10.20/.40, quartz digital watch movements (9108.12.00), several clock movements (9109.10.10, .30, .60, .70, 9109.90.40), metal and textile watch bands (9113.20.20, 9113.20.40, 9113.90.40) and a few others. USTR kept the lists after its 2026 review, and none of the product exclusions still in force (note 20(vvv), (www)) names a Chapter 91 product. changes.title: No Chapter 91 base rate changed
changes.detail: All 177 Chapter 91 rate lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, including the compound watch rates on the movement, case, strap and battery and the 9110 "rate applicable to the complete, assembled movement".

changes.title: China Section 301 lists continue after the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the 2018–2019 China Section 301 actions did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries. For Chapter 91 this keeps +7.5% (List 4A) on most Chinese watches, movements, cases, straps and parts, and +25% (List 3) on instrument-panel clocks, time recorders and time switches.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies — Swiss and Japanese watches 12.5% in total
changes.detail: Every Chapter 91 line from the 60 listed economies pays the duty (9903.05.20–9903.05.84); only civil-aircraft clocks and clock movements are exempt (note 52(d)). Switzerland and Japan pay 12.5% in total and the EU and Taiwan 10% in total where the base rate is lower — for a compound watch rate, measured by its ad valorem equivalent (note 52(k)). Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore and Hong Kong pay +12.5%; the UK, India, Malaysia, Mexico and Canada +10%. USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). China pays +12.5% on top of its List 3 or 4A duty.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), civil-aircraft goods excepted (9903.05.05). From July 24 the 12.5% tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top. Brazil supplied little Chapter 91 trade in 2025.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the Section 301 duty on Mexican and Canadian time switches, clocks and parts.

changes.title: CBP suspends de minimis indefinitely
changes.detail: Two interim final rules suspend the $800 de minimis exemption in CBP's regulations (19 CFR 10.151(b) for every mode except mail, 19 CFR 145.31(b) for mail) until CBP announces otherwise. A watch or strap bought online from abroad needs a formal or informal entry and pays the base rate plus any extra duty.
changes.before: Free under de minimis up to $800

changes.title: CBP opens CAPE for IEEPA duty refunds
changes.detail: Importers of record and their brokers can file a CAPE Declaration in ACE listing entries that paid IEEPA duties — for example the 39% and later 15%-in-total duty on Swiss watches — and ACE refunds the IEEPA duties with interest. The Section 301 duties and the Section 122 surcharge are not refunded.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026, on top of the base rate. No watch, clock or part was on the product exemption list; civil-aircraft clocks were exempt (9903.03.05), and so were USMCA-qualifying goods of Canada and Mexico. A $5,000 Swiss steel automatic watch paid $566.53 instead of $750.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028, on every Chapter 91 line. Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: Swiss watches: 39% cut to 15% in total
changes.detail: Under the U.S.–Switzerland–Liechtenstein framework, Swiss and Liechtenstein goods paid the higher of the base rate or 15% (base rate and reciprocal duty together) instead of the base rate + 39%, for goods entered from November 14, 2025. Watches were not exempted; civil-aircraft clocks of 9104 were. A $5,000 Swiss steel automatic watch paid $750 instead of $2,016.53. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Japanese watches: reciprocal tariff set at 15% in total
changes.detail: Executive Order 14345 set the reciprocal tariff on Japanese goods with a column 1 rate under 15% at 15% in total, applied to goods entered from August 7, 2025. A $200 Japanese quartz watch paid $30. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: De minimis suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free de minimis treatment for shipments of any value, origin or mode, so watches and straps under $800 ordered from abroad became dutiable. Executive Order 14388 continued the suspension after the IEEPA ruling.
changes.before: Free under de minimis up to $800

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline — Swiss watches +39%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Switzerland +39%, India +25%, Taiwan and Vietnam +20%, Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia +19%, the UK +10%; EU goods paid 15% in total. Watches, clocks and parts were not exempt. A $5,000 Swiss steel automatic watch paid $2,016.53 ($66.53 + 39%). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025. With the 20% fentanyl duty and the 7.5% List 4A duty, a Chinese quartz watch paid the base rate + 152.5% until May 13, 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025 on every Chapter 91 line, including Swiss, Japanese and EU watches; Canada and Mexico excluded. Higher country rates were paused until August 7, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the List 3 and List 4A duties. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from March 7. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10) from March 4, 2025, raised to +35% from August 1, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt from March 7. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: USTR halved the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) from 15% to 7.5% under the Phase One agreement. It still applies to most Chinese watches, movements, cases, straps and parts.

changes.title: China List 4A reaches watches, movements and parts
changes.detail: The fourth China Section 301 list put +15% on Chinese watches (9101, 9102), watch and clock movements (9108–9110), cases, straps and parts (9111–9114), and some clocks.

changes.title: China List 3 duty raised to 25%
changes.detail: USTR raised the List 3 duty (9903.88.03) from 10% to 25%. In Chapter 91 it covers instrument-panel clocks (9104.00.05–9104.00.50), time recorders, parking meters and interval timers (9106) and time switches (9107).

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 reaches clocks, time recorders and time switches
changes.detail: The third China Section 301 list put +10% on Chinese instrument-panel clocks, time recorders, parking meters and time switches.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 91 goods were **$6.77B in 2025**, 12.6% less than the $7.74B of 2024 and 58% more than in 2020. Watches dominate: heading 9102 (cases other than precious metal) $4.55B and heading 9101 (precious-metal cases) $1.61B. The largest single line is automatic watches with a steel or other case (9102.21, $3.26B), ahead of automatic gold watches (9101.21, $1.25B) and quartz watches with hands (9102.11, $841M).

**Switzerland** supplied $5.52B (81.6%), down 14.7% from $6.47B in 2024. In 2025 Swiss watches paid IEEPA duties from April 5 (10%, then 39% from August 7 and 15% in total from November 14). Gold-cased watches fell most: 9101.21 dropped 27.6%. **Japan** ($445M) ships mostly 9102 watches. **China** ($400M) ships cheaper watches, straps ($100M), clocks ($91.5M) and time switches. **Mexico** ($71.8M, up 72%) ships almost only time switches (9107), most of them Free under USMCA. Germany, Thailand, France and Singapore follow.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the 10% Section 122 surcharge to July 23 and the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro: Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For watches the country matters more than the base rate. **Swiss and Japanese** watches pay **12.5% of their value in total** (9903.05.74, 9903.05.49), and **EU and Taiwanese** watches **10%** (9903.05.39, 9903.05.76): the compound base rate of a watch is almost always worth less than that, so the flat rate replaces it. From **Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore and Hong Kong** the base rate is charged and **12.5%** is added; from the **UK, India and Malaysia**, 10%. **China** adds 12.5% plus 7.5% (List 4A) on most watches and parts, or 25% (List 3) on time switches, time recorders and instrument-panel clocks. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada pay nothing.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-13, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.
Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; SG for Singapore. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.

Compound base rates ("$1.53 each + 4.2% on the case + 2% on the strap, band or bracelet") are charged on the value of each component, which the importer declares on its statistical-note-1 number (for 9102.21.90: movement 9102.21.9010, case .9020, strap .9030). Each such line is listed under its first statistical number, and the tariff calculator prices it from the component values entered for those numbers. The cells use nominal component values and keep the component terms in words; for Switzerland, Japan, the EU and Taiwan the "in total" rate is compared with the ad valorem equivalent of the base rate (note 52(k)), shown as "the higher of".

Movement sets (9110.11, 9110.90.20) pay the rate of the complete movement, which the importer names; those cells show the rule in words. Movement parts with a plate (9110.90.40, 9114.90.30) are capped at the duty on the complete movement; the cells show the uncapped rate with the cap in words.

EU, Switzerland, Japan and Taiwan "in total" rules: where the base rate is below 10% (EU, Taiwan) or 12.5% (Switzerland, Japan), the total is that figure; lines at or above it pay only their base rate.

Not in the cells: the insular-possessions watch program (additional U.S. note 5, 15 CFR part 303), the civil-aircraft exemption (note 52(d)), FTA preferences of countries not listed, and the Section 232 certified-parts elections, which are opt-in. No antidumping or countervailing duty order and no Section 232 duty covers a Chapter 91 product.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 2, 16, 19, 20, 30, 31, 33, 36–39, 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. The only Chapter 99 lists that name Chapter 91 lines are the civil-aircraft lists — note 52(d) (9903.05.88), note 50(a)(iv) for Brazil (9903.05.05), note 51(d) for Canada and the expired Section 122 list (9903.03.05) — which cover instrument-panel clocks 9104.00.05–9104.00.60 and clock movements 9109.10.50, 9109.10.60 and 9109.90.20 for civil aircraft. The general exemption list (note 52(b)), the product list in note 52(c) and every country exception list in note 52(j) — EU, Switzerland, UK, Malaysia, Taiwan and the others — name no Chapter 91 line. The Canada Section 338 lists (note 51(b)) name none. China: List 3 (9903.88.03) covers 9104.00.05–9104.00.50, 9106 and 9107; List 4A (9903.88.15) covers most other lines; the lines on neither include 9103.10.20/.40, most of 9105.11, 9105.21 and 9105.91, 9108.12.00, 9108.90.80, several clock movements and 9113.20.20/.40 and 9113.90.40. The product exclusions still in force (note 20(vvv), (www), through November 9, 2026) name no Chapter 91 product; the watch-case, dial and kitchen-timer exclusions in earlier subdivisions have expired. No note 31 increase, Russia note 30 line or Section 232 list names a Chapter 91 line. A Federal Register search found no antidumping or countervailing duty order on watches, clocks or their parts.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 91: Watches, Clocks and Parts — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Watches into the U.S.: Watch Marking Rules, Component Valuation, Country of Origin & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 91) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 91 line needs at U.S. entry — the special watch and clock marking rules (additional U.S. note 4, 19 CFR 11.9), component values under statistical note 1, origin by movement, wildlife rules for exotic-leather straps — and the legal ways to pay less: classification, origin, USMCA, repairs abroad, the insular-possessions program, drawback and FTZs.
keywords: clocks and watches and parts thereof tariff
mexico tariff on clocks and watches and parts thereof

tariffEngineering.intro:
Watches and clocks need no import license, but they have **their own marking rule**. Every movement and case — imported alone or inside a watch or clock — must be marked by cutting, die-sinking, engraving, stamping or mold-marking with the country of manufacture, the name of the manufacturer or purchaser and, on movements, the number of jewels (additional U.S. note 4); CBP will not release unmarked goods (19 CFR 11.9). Quartz watches with a digital display only are excepted. The entry must also **split each watch into its components** — movement, case, strap, battery — with a value for each (statistical note 1), because the compound rate is charged on those values.

On cost, the main lever is the **country of origin**, which for a watch is where the **movement was assembled**: a Swiss watch pays 12.5% of value, an EU one 10%, a Chinese one the base rate + 20%. USMCA, the insular-possessions program, repairs abroad (9802), drawback and foreign-trade zones can lower it further.

levers.title: Declare each component's value correctly
levers.saves: The duty on the case, strap and battery percentages: on a $5,000 watch of 9102.21.70, moving $500 of value from a steel bracelet (9.8%) to the movement (charged per piece) changes the base rate by $49 — but only where the base rate is charged (not for Swiss, Japanese, EU or Taiwanese watches, which pay a flat 12.5% or 10% of the whole value)
levers.appliesTo: Compound-rate watches and clocks of 9101–9105, 9108 and 9109
levers.document: Supplier invoices or cost breakdowns that value the movement, case, strap and battery separately.
levers.caveat: The values must reflect what the components are worth. CBP rejected an importer's allocation that put brand, profit and overhead on the movement and reapportioned the entries (HQ H326900).

levers.title: Classify by case, movement, jewels and strap material
levers.saves: Up to the whole base rate: a mechanical watch with a gold case and over 17 jewels (9101.21.50) is Free, one with a steel case (9102.21.70) pays $1.53 + 4.2% of the case + 9.8% of a steel bracelet; a leather strap entered on its own pays 1.8% (9113.90.80), a steel bracelet 11.2% (9113.20)
levers.document: Technical sheets: case material, movement type, jewel count, movement size, display type, strap material.
levers.caveat: Heading 9101 needs a case wholly of precious metal (chapter note 2); a steel case inlaid with gold is 9102. A strap entered with the watch goes with the watch (additional U.S. note 2). Smartwatches are not Chapter 91 — CBP classifies them in 8517.62 (NY N349122).

citations.label: HTSUS Chapter 91, notes 2–3 and additional U.S. notes 1–3

levers.title: Know the country of origin — where the movement was assembled
levers.saves: The gap between country rates: a $5,000 steel automatic pays $500 from the EU, $625 from Switzerland or Japan, $691.53 from Thailand or Hong Kong and $1,066.53 from China
levers.appliesTo: All watches; for clocks and parts, the usual substantial-transformation rule
levers.document: Production records showing where the movement was assembled and where the strap was made.
levers.caveat: CBP's long-standing position is that a watch (without its strap) originates where the movement is assembled; casing, dial and hands do not change it (NY N364461, NY N351984). A Japanese movement cased in China makes a Japanese watch; a strap keeps its own origin.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Mexican and Canadian clocks, time switches and parts
levers.saves: The base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty: a qualifying Mexican time switch enters Free
levers.appliesTo: Goods of Mexico and Canada that meet the USMCA rules of origin (SPI S)
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin (19 CFR 182.12) kept with the entry records.
levers.caveat: Most watches are not made in North America; the claim helps time switches (9107), clocks and parts.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Assemble watches in the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam or American Samoa
levers.saves: The whole base rate: licensed insular watches and movements enter Free regardless of foreign parts, within the annual quantity; producers can also earn duty-refund certificates
levers.document: A license and shipment permit from Commerce and Interior (15 CFR part 303); producers apply on form ITA-334P.
levers.caveat: The goods may contain no material from a column 2 country, and must meet the minimum assembly rules. The last published allocation (calendar 2015) gave the USVI 1,866,000 units and found no producers in Guam, American Samoa or the Northern Mariana Islands.

levers.title: Use Chapter 98 for repairs abroad and U.S. goods returned
levers.saves: Duty on everything but the repair: a watch sent abroad for service pays duty, including the Section 301 duty, only on the value of the repair (9802.00.40 for warranty repairs, 9802.00.50 for others); U.S. goods, or foreign goods within 3 years of export, returned unchanged enter Free (9801.00.10) with no Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: Watches and clocks exported for repair or alteration, or returned
levers.document: Proof of export (CBP Form 4455 or equivalent) and the repairer's invoice for the work (19 CFR 10.8).
levers.caveat: Note 52(a) charges the Section 301 duty on the value of the repairs for 9802.00.40/.50 entries; other Chapter 98 entries such as 9801.00.10 are outside it. The watch must come back the same article, not exchanged for another.

provisions.rate: Duty on the value of repairs
provisions.text: Repairs or alterations made pursuant to a warranty

provisions.rate: Duty on the value of repairs or alterations
provisions.text: Articles exported for repairs or alterations
U.S. goods, or other goods within 3 years of export, returned without being advanced in value

levers.title: Bring samples in temporarily — TIB or ATA carnet
levers.saves: All duty on watches imported for a trade show or to take orders, if re-exported
levers.document: A temporary importation bond (9813.00) or an ATA carnet.
levers.caveat: The goods must be exported within the bond period (one year, extendable) and not sold.

levers.title: Claim drawback on re-exported watches
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, including the Section 301 duty, when the watches (or interchangeable ones) are exported
levers.appliesTo: Watches, movements and parts that are exported or destroyed
levers.document: Import and export records and a drawback claim in ACE (19 CFR part 190).
levers.caveat: Substitution needs commercially interchangeable goods (CBP has ruled on watch models); file within five years of import.

levers.title: Hold stock in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: Defers duty until goods leave the zone for the U.S. market; none on goods re-exported
levers.appliesTo: Distributors holding inventory for the U.S. and export markets
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's records.
levers.caveat: Goods admitted after the 2026 Section 301 duty generally enter in privileged-foreign status and pay the duty when they leave the zone.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before the first shipment
levers.saves: Certainty on classification, origin and component reporting
levers.appliesTo: New models, multi-country supply chains, smart or hybrid watches
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP (19 CFR part 177).
levers.caveat: A ruling binds only for the facts described in it.

rules.title: Watch and clock movements, cases and dials must carry the special marking — country of manufacture, manufacturer or purchaser (full name or registered trade name) and, on movements, the number of jewels in words — by cutting, die-sinking, engraving, stamping or mold-marking; unmarked goods are not released and owe a 10% marking duty unless marked, exported or destroyed

Every article is marked with its country of origin; a watch takes the origin of its movement, and a strap made in another country must be marked with its own origin (a hangtag that stays on until sale is acceptable)

Watches, clocks and movements with compound rates are entered component by component — movement, case, strap, band or bracelet, battery — each on its own statistical suffix with its own value, the values adding up to the article's value; CBP reapportions values that are not supported (the tariff calculator asks for the same component values)
Straps of alligator, crocodile, ostrich, lizard or other wildlife leather need a Fish and Wildlife declaration (Form 3-177) and, for CITES-listed species, the CITES documents

rules.agency: Federal Trade Commission / Department of Justice
rules.title: Gold watchcases stamped with a fineness mark must not fall short of it by more than three one-thousandths (15 U.S.C. 295); falsely marked gold or silver goods may not be imported for sale (15 U.S.C. 294)

Report the Chapter 99 heading that applies to the origin — the 2026 Section 301 country heading (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), the USMCA or civil-aircraft exemption heading, and for China the List 3 or 4A heading — with the Chapter 91 line

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20 and 52

groups.label: Watches with precious-metal case
groups.note: Movement and case must carry the note 4 marking; a gold case's fineness mark must be accurate. Swiss and Japanese gold watches pay 12.5% of value; exotic-leather straps need a wildlife declaration.

groups.label: Watches with other case (steel, titanium, plastic)
groups.note: Enter movement, case, strap and battery on their own suffixes with their values. Quartz watches with a digital display only are excepted from the note 4 marking.

groups.label: Clocks with watch movements
groups.note: Movement and case marking (note 4); travel clocks and other clocks report movement, case and battery separately.

groups.label: Instrument-panel clocks for vehicles, aircraft and vessels
groups.note: Civil-aircraft clocks meeting general note 6 are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; Chinese panel clocks pay 25% (List 3).

groups.label: Alarm, wall and other clocks
groups.note: Clock movements and cases carry the note 4 marking; clocks that run only on AC power report as one unit.

groups.label: Time recorders, parking meters and interval timers
groups.note: No special marking beyond origin unless a clock movement is inside. Chinese time recorders pay 25% (List 3).

groups.label: Time switches
groups.note: USMCA-qualifying Mexican time switches enter Free with no Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Watch movements, complete and assembled
groups.note: Each movement marked on a bridge or top plate with country, maker and jewels in words.

groups.label: Clock movements, complete and assembled
groups.note: Clock movements marked on the front or back plate. Civil-aircraft movements of 9109.10.50, 9109.10.60 and 9109.90.20 are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Movement sets, incomplete and rough movements, movement parts
groups.note: A movement set pays the rate of the complete movement — name that line at entry. Parts with a plate are capped at the complete movement's duty.

groups.label: Watch cases and parts
groups.note: Watch cases marked inside or outside the back with country and maker; gold cases must meet their fineness mark.

groups.label: Clock cases and parts
groups.note: Clock cases marked on the outside of the back with the country of manufacture.

groups.label: Watch straps, bands and bracelets
groups.note: Straps marked with their own origin; exotic leather needs a wildlife declaration.

groups.label: Other clock and watch parts (dials, plates, springs, jewels)
groups.note: Dials and plates for movements follow the note 4 marking when imported separately (19 CFR 11.9 names dials); jewels are Free.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations and the tariff schedule — not legal advice. The line a watch falls in, the value of each component, the origin of a movement and the Chapter 99 duties that apply depend on the facts of each shipment, and the extra duties change by Federal Register notice and CBP guidance; confirm the current headings and marking before each shipment.

finalConclusion.h1: HTS Chapter 91: Watches, Clocks and Parts — Tariff FAQ

seo.title: Watch Tariff FAQ 2026: Swiss Watch Tariff, Japan, China & Hong Kong Rates, Watch HS Codes (HTS Ch. 91) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. tariffs on watches and clocks: the current Swiss watch tariff, whether the 39% still applies, refunds, watches from Japan, China and Hong Kong, used watches, how watch duty is calculated, and the HS codes for watches, straps, parts, clocks and smartwatches.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for watches, clocks, movements, straps and parts. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Chapter 91 base rates have not changed: most watches pay a compound rate — a charge per movement plus percentages on the case, strap and battery — and many gold mechanical watches are Free.

Since July 24, 2026 Swiss and Japanese watches pay 12.5% of their value in total and EU and Taiwanese watches 10% (Section 301, note 52(k)); Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore and Hong Kong add 12.5% to the base rate; the UK, India and Malaysia 10%.
Chinese watches pay the base rate + 12.5% + 7.5% (List 4A); Chinese time switches, time recorders and panel clocks the base rate + 37.5%.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs — 39% on Swiss watches from August 7, 2025, then 15% in total — ended February 24, 2026; importers can claim refunds through CBP's CAPE process. The 10% Section 122 surcharge ran from February 24 to July 23, 2026.
A watch's origin is where its movement was assembled; every movement and case must carry the special marking of additional U.S. note 4.
Smartwatches are not Chapter 91: CBP classifies them in 8517.62.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on Swiss watches now?
searchedAs: are rolex watches subject to tariffs
faqs.answer: Since July 24, 2026, Swiss watches pay 12.5% of their customs value in total. The Section 301 heading for Switzerland (9903.05.74) replaces the base rate with 12.5% whenever the base rate is lower, and for a watch's compound rate it almost always is — a $5,000 steel automatic owes $66.53 at the base rate (1.3%). So that watch pays $625, and a $30,000 gold watch $3,750. Swiss watch movements, straps and parts pay 12.5% too. Switzerland's exception list names no Chapter 91 product.

faqs.question: Does the 39% tariff on Swiss watches still apply?
faqs.answer: No. The 39% IEEPA reciprocal rate applied to Swiss goods entered from August 7, 2025, on top of the base rate. From November 14, 2025 it was cut to 15% in total under the U.S.–Switzerland framework. All IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, after the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. Swiss watches then paid the base rate + 10% (Section 122) until July 23, 2026, and 12.5% in total since July 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Can I get a refund of the tariffs paid on Swiss watches in 2025?
faqs.answer: The IEEPA duties — the 10%, 39% and 15%-in-total rates on Swiss watches in 2025–2026 — are being refunded. Since April 20, 2026 the importer of record (or its broker) can file a CAPE Declaration in ACE listing the entries, and CBP refunds the IEEPA duty with interest. The Section 122 surcharge and the Section 301 duties are not refunded. A consumer who bought from a retailer is not the importer of record.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on watches from Japan?
searchedAs: tariff on watches from japan to usa
us tariff on watches from japan
what is the current tariff on watches from japan
are there tariffs on watches from japan
tariff on swiss watches from japan
faqs.answer: Japanese watches pay 12.5% of their value in total (9903.05.49): a $200 quartz watch pays $25. What counts is the watch's origin — the country where its movement was assembled — not where it was bought or shipped from, so a Swiss watch bought in Japan still pays the Swiss rate (also 12.5%), and a watch with a Japanese movement cased in China is Japanese.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on watches from China?
searchedAs: china tariff on clocks and watches
faqs.answer: Most Chinese watches pay the base rate + 12.5% (2026 Section 301) + 7.5% (List 4A): $46.11 on a $200 quartz watch with hands. Chinese time switches, time recorders and instrument-panel clocks pay the base rate + 12.5% + 25% (List 3). Some alarm and wall clocks and metal watch bands are on neither list and pay the base rate + 12.5%. The 2025 IEEPA duties (up to 145%) have ended.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on watches from Hong Kong?
searchedAs: tariff on watches from hong kong
us tariff on 6500 watch from hong kong
faqs.answer: A watch of Hong Kong origin pays the base rate + 12.5% (9903.05.43); Hong Kong goods are not on the China Section 301 lists. But origin is where the movement was assembled: a Swiss watch bought from a Hong Kong dealer pays the Swiss rate, 12.5% of value — $812.50 on a $6,500 watch — and a watch with a Chinese movement pays the China rate.

faqs.question: Are watches exempt from tariffs?
searchedAs: are swiss watches exempt from tariffs
are swiss watches subject to tariffs
faqs.answer: No. No watch, clock or part is on the Section 301 general exemption list or on any country's exception list; the only Chapter 91 goods exempted are instrument-panel clocks and clock movements for civil aircraft. Watches were not exempt from the 2025 reciprocal tariff or the 2026 Section 122 surcharge either. Goods from countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies, and USMCA-qualifying goods, pay only the base rate.

faqs.question: Do used or pre-owned watches pay tariffs?
searchedAs: are used watches subject to tariffs
tariff on used watches from japan
faqs.answer: Yes. A used watch is classified and charged like a new one — its origin is still where the movement was assembled, so a pre-owned Swiss watch bought in Japan pays 12.5% of its value. A watch exported from the U.S. and returned unchanged within 3 years can enter Free (9801.00.10), and a watch sent abroad for repair pays duty only on the repair (9802.00.40 or 9802.00.50).

faqs.question: How is import duty on a watch calculated?
faqs.answer: Most watch rates are compound: a charge per movement (for example $1.53) plus a percentage of the case value, of the strap value and, for quartz watches, of the battery value. The entry lists each component on its own statistical suffix with its value (statistical note 1). Then the country rule applies: Swiss and Japanese watches pay 12.5% of the whole value if that is more than the base rate, EU watches 10%; others pay the base rate plus their Section 301 rate. The KoalaGains tariff calculator asks for the value of each component on its statistical-note-1 number and prices the total. Since de minimis is suspended, every watch shipped from abroad pays.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for watches?
faqs.answer: Wrist and pocket watches are heading 9101 if the case is wholly of precious metal and 9102 otherwise. The next digits depend on the movement (electric with hands 9101.11/9102.11, digital 9101.19/9102.12, automatic 9101.21/9102.21, manual 9101.29/9102.29), the jewels, the movement size and value and the strap material. A steel automatic with over 17 jewels and a steel bracelet is 9102.21.70; with a rubber or leather strap 9102.21.90; with a gold case 9101.21.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a watch strap or band?
searchedAs: hs code for leather watch strap
hs code for rubber watch strap
faqs.answer: A strap entered with its watch is classified with the watch. On its own it is heading 9113: precious metal 9113.10 (4.5%), base-metal bracelets 9113.20 (11.2%), textile straps 9113.90.40 (7.2%) and leather, rubber and other straps 9113.90.80 (1.8%). The Section 301 rate for the country is added (Swiss and Japanese 12.5% in total).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for watch parts and movements?
faqs.answer: Complete watch movements are 9108, clock movements 9109, movement sets and incomplete movements 9110, watch cases 9111, clock cases 9112 and other parts — dials, plates, springs, jewels, hands — 9114. A battery entered with a watch or movement goes with it; otherwise it is heading 8506 or 8507.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a smartwatch or Apple Watch?
faqs.answer: Smartwatches are not Chapter 91. CBP classifies them as apparatus for the transmission or reception of data, 8517.62.00.90 (NY N349122, Free base rate), so the Chapter 91 watch rates and marking rules do not apply; the country's Section 301 rate does.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for clocks?
faqs.answer: Alarm clocks are 9105.11–9105.19, wall clocks 9105.21–9105.29 and other clocks (including cuckoo, mantel and table clocks) 9105.91–9105.99; clocks built on a watch movement are 9103 and vehicle or aircraft dashboard clocks 9104. Rates are per clock plus a percentage of the case and battery values.
